en.g: a female given name from Danish [in turn from Old Norse], equivalent to English Bodil

1004485.etyen:
An orthographic variant of Bodil, which was Danish Bodil, ultimately from Old Norse Bóthildr, a female given name formed from bót (“remedy, help, improvement”) and hildr (“battle, fight”).
The spelling Bodill also has historical precedent in Danish. It is attested alongside Bodil, Bodild and Bodel in 18th- and 19th-century Danish records.

en.g: a cross, often bearing an image of the crucified Christ; a crucifix
x: Et gammelt rodekors hang over inngangen til koret.
An old rood cross hung above the entrance to the chancel.
Biskop Sigurd ... satte et Rode-Kors op i Stavnen ...
Bishop Sigurd ... set up a rood cross in the bow ...

1004997.etyen:
Compound of rode (“rood, cross, crucifix”) + kors (“cross”), literally “rood cross”. The formation corresponds closely to Old Norse róðukross (“crucifix”), itself formed from róða (“cross, crucifix”) and kross (“cross”).
The first element rode (“rood, cross, crucifix”) is archaizing, after Old Norse róða, and belongs to the same Germanic word family as Old English rōd (“rod, pole; cross”). These forms continue Proto-Germanic *rōdō (“rod, pole”) (also *rōdǭ in northern Germanic). The deeper origin is uncertain; Proto-Germanic *rōdō has been compared with Proto-Indo-European *reh₁t- (“post”).
